history.titleZh: 中国阿里巴巴再次挑战美国AI霸主地位
history.descriptionZh:
阿里巴巴于本周一正式发布了其迄今为止规模最大、号称“能力最强”的AI模型Qwen3.8-Max，并宣布向用户广泛开放。该公司在一篇博客文章中表示，该模型的性能足以媲美美国前沿实验室Anthropic和OpenAI的顶级系统，以及国内竞争对手月之暗面（Moonshot AI）的Kimi K3。此前在上个月的预告中，阿里巴巴曾声称该模型“仅次于Anthropic的旗舰产品Fable 5”，本次发布可谓在预期之内。

Qwen3.8-Max的开放发布，再度加剧了硅谷与华盛顿在多个维度的高度紧张——既涉及如何安全管理AI系统，也关乎美国能否维持对华技术优势。据阿里巴巴周一公布的内部测试结果，该模型实力确如其宣称，在众包模型对比平台Arena.AI上的排名也印证了这一点。自家评测显示，在基准测试中Qwen3.8-Max的表现总体上与Fable 5持平，部分项目甚至有所超越。在Arena文本模型排行榜上，Qwen3.8-Max仅次于Fable 5及Anthropic Opus系列中的三款模型；在前端编码任务中，仅落后于两款Claude Opus模型和Kimi K3；在视觉分析任务中，只有Fable 5能胜过它。

阿里巴巴表示，Qwen3.8-Max拥有2.4万亿参数。参数是衡量模型在训练中习得的“设置”数量的数值指标，用于处理数据、识别模式和执行各类任务。尽管参数数量常被当作模型性能的粗略指标，但更大的数字并不必然意味着更强。月之暗面的Kimi K3参数规模达2.8万亿，而大多数美国顶尖实验室对具体数字讳莫如深，OpenAI和Anthropic均未披露其顶级旗舰模型的准确参数。

这家中国科技巨头还透露，将于下周发布Qwen3.8-Max的权重。权重是决定AI如何处理信息的可调数值，开放权重系统虽比传统开源软件更具限制性，却能让开发者获得远超OpenAI、Anthropic等闭源产品的控制力。值得注意的是，Qwen3.8-Max标志着阿里巴巴在短暂转向专有发布策略后，重新回归开放权重路线。今年早些时候，该公司曾对其更先进的模型采用闭源方式。

开放权重正日益成为中国AI产业的差异化优势，并已成为行业常态。月之暗面上周已发布Kimi K3，许多其他顶尖中国AI模型同样开放权重。北京方面积极倡导这一策略，以此扩大中国在全球AI治理中的影响力，并推动本土科技领军企业获得更广泛的应用。阿里巴巴此次发布进一步加剧了竞争——中国公司正迅速缩小与美国同行的差距，并明显加快发布节奏。Qwen3.8-Max紧随Kimi K3之后问世，后者同样被视为对美国AI主导地位的一次挑战；此外，字节跳动和MiniMax也于上周五发布了功能强大的新一代视频生成模型。

开放性本身也已成为一个颇具争议的话题。在中国密集发布开放权重模型后，美国有报道称可能对开放工具采取限制措施，但美国业界大体上一致支持保留开放权重模型的访问权，这既是出于安全必要，也是维持竞争的手段。与此形成对照的是，闭源模型提供商（尤其是OpenAI和Anthropic）正面临越来越严格的审视，原因是它们披露了一系列由自身失控AI代理无意中实施的网络攻击。来自某受害者的事件报告表明，旨在阻止AI模型被恶意使用的严格安全护栏，反而限制了这些模型作为防御工具的效能。

总体而言，Qwen3.8-Max的发布是中国AI能力持续跃升的标志性事件。凭借其媲美美国顶尖闭源模型的基准表现、庞大参数规模以及开放权重策略，它既为全球开发者提供了强大的开源替代方案，也在前沿编码、视觉分析等垂直场景中展现出直接应用潜力。与此同时，围绕开放与封闭、安全与竞争的全球博弈，正随着此类模型的不断涌现而愈发激烈。

history.content: Fender CEO Edward “Bud” Cole gave an interview to T3 in May celebrating the 75th anniversary of the Telecaster with comments on AI and music that initially flew under the radar. But it has started making the rounds recently, pouring more fuel on an already raging fire of bad PR following the company pissing off basically the entire guitar-playing community by sending cease-and-desist letters to builders, claiming copyright of the Stratocaster body shape.Some influential guitar YouTubers have even said they’re done buying Fender gear in the wake of the controversy. And Cole’s resurfaced comments comparing cover songs and bandmates to a sort of “analog AI” have only sunk the company’s standing further among the loudest of its fans online.T3 editor-in-chief Mat Gallagher’s feature mostly paraphrases Cole’s statements, and Fender did not immediately respond to a request for comment or clarification. But here are the relevant bits from the interview:Cole’s philosophy is that AI in music is nothing new. “I think AI has existed in music as long as there’s been recorded music,” he says. While the biggest barrier to playing guitar is the time it takes to learn the instrument, it’s the second barrier, writing songs, where he believes AI plays a part.“I actually believe cover music has been sort of analog AI for a long time,” says Cole. Those that don’t yet have the skills to write their own songs can play the songs written by their favourite artists instead. “I listened a lot to REM, U2, The Smiths and The Cure, and at some point I got sick of just listening to them. I wanted to play it, so I learned to play guitar.”Those taking their first steps into writing, according to Cole, can also lean on a second analogue form of AI: their band mates. You might just have a chorus or a riff to start with but then the drummer or bassist can add to it, and a song is born. AI can also play this role. “I actually think that we are in the brink of freeing up people to move beyond the same old covers and to really get into working like they do with their bands,” says Cole.Cole is trying to draw a comparison between a human “training” on a handful of cover songs and an AI ingesting enormous datasets of copyrighted music. He appears to be suggesting that, by learning to play other people’s songs, internalizing those influences, and then synthesizing them into something new, you are essentially doing the same thing as an AI. This is a woefully misguided take that says to me that Cole either doesn’t understand AI or doesn’t respect artists.For starters, scale matters. No person could possibly learn all of the songs used to train your average generative AI model, which, in the case of Suno, is suspected to be in the millions. Additionally, it dismisses the inherent humanity of the millions of tiny decisions, conscious or otherwise, that an artist makes during the songwriting process. Whether they’re driven by emotional response, reacting to a happy accident, or compensating for limitations, the artistic decisions made by a human are unique to them.This is fundamentally different from a model spitting out something based on a prompt and a network of data points. As Steve Onotera, better known as Samurai Guitarist, points out, a player’s physicality, or the tiny errors that every human is prone to, prevent them from replicating someone else’s work perfectly. That kind of serendipity can’t be replicated by an LLM.The same is true of bandmates. Humans who pull from their own unique sets of “training data,” life experiences, and physical skills or limitations are not the same as a chatbot. An AI doesn’t have taste or instincts in the way that your picky bassist who studied jazz composition in college does. If you told your drummer they were no different from an AI model, they’d rightfully be insulted.Later in the interview, Cole says: “I believe that AI is actually going to help create a whole new world of guitar players that use it. To help connect with other musicians, to be more productive. And across the chasm into becoming a student of songwriting to a master of songwriting.”Cole’s assertion that AI will somehow help people “across the chasm” to becoming master songwriters is also, frankly, ridiculous. Evidence is mounting that relying on AI tools is actually leading to deskilling. Using an AI to suggest rhymes or metaphors for pain isn’t the same as practicing songwriting and developing skills. The AI has never been left at the altar or sweated over the perfect pre-chorus transition. Repetition is the key. The adage is that you need to write 100 (or 1,000) (or 10,000) bad songs before you write one good one. That’s how you grow beyond tired tropes and learn to recognize when you’ve stumbled into something good.

history.titleZh: Fender 的 CEO 似乎认为你的乐队伙伴只是模拟 AI
history.descriptionZh:
Fender CEO爱德华·“巴德”·科尔在5月接受T3杂志采访时，为庆祝Telecaster吉他75周年发表了对AI与音乐的评论，当时并未引起太多关注。但近日这段言论在网络上重新传播，给公司本已糟糕的公众形象火上浇油——此前Fender向众多制琴师发送停止侵权函，声称拥有Stratocaster琴体形状的版权，激怒了整个吉他社区。一些有影响力的吉他YouTuber甚至表示，在这起争议之后不再购买Fender产品。而科尔那段将翻唱歌曲和乐队成员比作某种“模拟AI”的言论，进一步损害了公司在网上最活跃粉丝心中的地位。

科尔的核心观点是，音乐中的AI并非新鲜事物。“我认为只要有录音音乐存在，AI就存在于音乐中。”他指出，学习吉他最大的障碍是时间投入，而第二个障碍是写歌，AI正是能在写歌环节发挥作用。“我实际上认为翻唱音乐长期以来就是某种模拟AI。”那些还不具备原创能力的人可以演奏他们最喜欢的艺术家的歌曲。科尔本人就是通过这种方式学习吉他的：“我听了很多REM、U2、The Smiths和The Cure的歌，后来我厌倦了只是听，我想去演奏，所以我学会了吉他。”

科尔认为，初学写歌的人也可以依靠第二种“模拟AI”：他们的乐队伙伴。你可能只有一段副歌或一个即兴重复段，但鼓手或贝斯手可以加进来，一首歌就诞生了。AI也能扮演这个角色。“我确实觉得我们正处在这样一个临界点：人们将被解放出来，不再局限于老套的翻唱，而是真正像和乐队合作那样去创作。”

然而，评论者指出科尔的类比存在根本性缺陷。他将人类学习几首翻唱歌曲的过程与AI摄取海量受版权保护的数据集相提并论，暗示人类通过学弹别人的歌曲、吸收影响然后综合成新作品，本质上与AI做的事情一样。这种观点被批评为对AI缺乏理解或对艺术家缺乏尊重。

首先，规模完全不同。没有任何人能够学完一个生成式AI模型训练所用的全部歌曲——以Suno为例，其训练数据据推测可能达数百万首。其次，这种类比抹杀了艺术家在创作过程中做出的数百万个微小决定所蕴含的人性，这些决定无论是有意识还是无意识的，都源于情感反应、对偶然意外的应对或对自身局限的补偿，是独一无二的。这与AI根据提示和数据点网络生成输出的本质完全不同。正如网红吉他手Steve Onotera（网名Samurai Guitarist）指出的，演奏者的身体条件以及每个人都有的人为微小失误，使他们无法完美复制他人的作品，这种“意外之喜”是大型语言模型无法复制的。

乐队成员的情况也是如此。人类拥有各自独特的“训练数据”、生活经历和身体技能或局限，这与聊天机器人截然不同。AI不具备那种品味和直觉——比如你那位在大学学过爵士作曲的挑剔贝斯手所拥有的东西。如果你告诉鼓手他和AI模型没什么区别，他完全有理由感到被冒犯。

科尔还宣称“AI将帮助创造一个新世界的吉他手，帮助他们与其他音乐家联系，提高生产力，跨越从歌曲创作学徒到大师的鸿沟。”这一说法也被认为荒谬。越来越多的证据表明，依赖AI工具实际上会导致技能退化。用AI来建议押韵或比喻痛苦，与练习写歌、培养技能完全不同。AI从未经历过在人生关键时刻的失落，也不曾为完美的预副歌过渡而绞尽脑汁。重复是关键所在。俗话说，你需要写100首（或1000首，或10000首）烂歌才能写出一首好歌。这正是你摆脱陈词滥调、学会识别自己偶然写出好作品的方式。

总而言之，这场争议揭示了音乐行业对AI态度的深层分歧：Fender试图将AI描绘成创作民主化的工具，但批评者认为这种类比不仅贬低了人类创作的价值，也忽视了AI在规模、本质和创造力上的根本差异。对于Fender这样拥有深厚文化底蕴的品牌而言，在AI浪潮中如何平衡技术创新与尊重艺术传统，已成为一个亟待解决的核心问题。
